Given these details, when connecting to the 'default' NATS server (which we understand to be `demo.nats.io` based on the context), the client library will use `demo.nats.io` as the URL format, but since the default port 4222 is used, the complete URL remains `nats://demo.nats.io:4222`.

[1] [3] By default, a NATS connection will echo messages if the connection also has interest in the published subject, meaning that if a publisher on a connection sends a message to a subject, any subscribers on that same connection will receive the message. To stop this behavior and ensure that messages are not delivered to subscribers on the same connection, you can opt to turn off this echo. This setting is per connection and not per application, so each connection must be configured to turn off echo. ![](../../../.gitbook/assets/noecho.svg) Keep in mind that turning echo on or off can result in a significant change to your applications communication protocol, as messages will flow or stop flowing based on this setting, and the subscribing code will not have any indication as to why. [2] [3] When a slow consumer is detected and messages are about to be dropped, the library may notify the application. This process may be similar to other errors or may involve a custom callback. Some libraries, like Java, will not send this notification on every dropped message because that could be noisy. Rather the notification may be sent once per time the subscriber gets behind. NATS does not hand messages to the callback in parallel; instead, it waits until the slow consumer can process the message before sending the next one. Some common patterns that help include buffering incoming messages for a subscription to give the application time to catch up, and providing a way to get a count of dropped messages so that applications can at least detect a problem is occurring.
